metadata.description: A guide to Shona sounds for English speakers. Learn these before diving into vocabulary.

englishVsShonaIntro.title: How Shona pronunciation works differently from English
points: Every vowel is pure — no gliding (English "o" glides toward "oo"; Shona "o" stays steady on one quality).
Every syllable gets roughly equal time — English is stress-timed (some syllables get swallowed); Shona is more syllable-timed.
The "r" is a tap — touch the tongue to the roof of the mouth once (like Spanish), not a curled American /r/.
Some consonants are implosive — "b" and "d" can involve a slight inward suck of air before the release.
Tone matters — the pitch pattern of a word can change its meaning; use audio and repeat until the melody feels natural.

introduction: Shona uses the Latin alphabet, so most letters sound like you'd expect. But there are about 12 sound combinations that don't exist in English. This guide teaches them step by step. Master these and you can pronounce ANY Shona word. Read 'How Shona pronunciation works differently from English' (above) once — it saves confusion later.

levels.title: Sounds You Already Know
levels.description: These Shona letters sound almost exactly like English. You're already 70% there!

sounds.tip: Always 'ah', never 'ay' like in 'cake'
sounds.commonMistake: Using English 'ay' (cake) instead of a steady 'ah' (father).

sounds.tip: Always 'eh', never 'ee' like in 'me'
sounds.commonMistake: Stretching toward English 'ee' (me) — keep it short like 'bet'.

sounds.tip: Always 'ee', never 'eye' like in 'mine'
sounds.commonMistake: Gliding to 'eye' — Shona /i/ is steady like 'see'.

sounds.tip: Always 'oh', never 'oo' like in 'moon'
sounds.commonMistake: Gliding to 'oo' — keep one clear 'oh' quality like 'more' without British rounding drift.

sounds.tip: Always 'oo', never 'uh' like in 'cup'
sounds.commonMistake: Using schwa 'uh' — Shona /u/ is a clear back 'oo'.

sounds.sound: b, d, f, g, h, k, m, n, p, r, s, t, v, w, y, z
sounds.englishAnchor: These sound the same as in English
sounds.tip: The 'r' is lightly rolled (like Spanish), not the English 'r'
sounds.commonMistake: Heavy English /r/, hard /b/ and /d/ plosives — Shona /r/ taps; /b/ and /d/ are often softer (implosive).

levels.title: Easy Combinations
levels.description: These combine familiar sounds in ways English doesn't. Once you hear the pattern, they click fast.

sounds.tip: Exactly like English 'ch' — easy!
sounds.commonMistake: None for most English speakers — same as 'church'.

sounds.tip: Exactly like English 'sh'
sounds.commonMistake: None for most English speakers — same as 'ship'.

sounds.englishAnchor: 'ds' in 'beds' — but at the START of a word
sounds.tip: Say 'beds' and notice the 'dz' at the end. Now put it at the beginning.
sounds.commonMistake: Inserting a vowel before word-initial 'dz' — go straight into the affricate.

sounds.tip: Like 'cats' but at the start. Practice: ca-ts → ts-oka
sounds.commonMistake: Adding 'uh' before syllable-initial 'ts' — start cleanly on the affricate.

sounds.tip: Same as 'sing' but at the start. Say 'si-ng' then drop the 'si'.
sounds.commonMistake: Using only the coda 'ng' of 'sing' when you need the 'finger'-type cluster, or adding 'uh-ng' at word onset.

sounds.tip: Like the 'ny' in 'canyon' or Spanish 'ñ'
sounds.commonMistake: Splitting into 'n' + 'y' as separate consonants — keep one smooth palatal nasal.

sounds.englishAnchor: Say 'z' then immediately 'v' — your lips buzz
sounds.tip: Start with 'z', let your bottom lip touch your top teeth for the 'v'. Quick combo.
sounds.commonMistake: Saying a normal English 'z' then 'v' with relaxed lips — the whistle comes from rounding during the fricative.

mouthPosition.lips: Rounded and slightly protruded, as if beginning to whistle
mouthPosition.tongue: Tip behind lower front teeth; blade raised for the voiced groove fricative
mouthPosition.airflow: Steady voiced friction with turbulent airflow; lip rounding raises the pitch of the buzz

sounds.tip: 's' flowing into 'v'. Like starting to say 'seven' but mashing s+v together.
sounds.commonMistake: Saying a normal 's' without lip rounding — the whistle quality comes from the lips.

mouthPosition.lips: Rounded, slightly protruded, as if about to whistle
mouthPosition.tongue: Tip behind lower teeth; blade raised toward the hard palate for a grooved fricative
mouthPosition.airflow: Air forced through a narrow groove with lip rounding — creates a higher, 'whistle-like' hiss

levels.title: Uniquely Shona Sounds
levels.description: These are the sounds that make Shona special. They don't exist in English, but they're not hard once you know the trick.

sounds.tip: Close your lips. Hum 'mmm' for a split second. Open into 'h'. It's like a breathy 'm'. Very common — you'll say this every day!
sounds.practice: Step 1: Hum 'mmm'. Step 2: While humming, push air out through your nose. Step 3: Open into 'horo'. Combined: mm-horo.
sounds.commonMistake: Saying 'm' then 'h' as separate letters — they blend into one breathy nasal.

mouthPosition.lips: Start closed for the hum, then open slightly with audible breathiness
mouthPosition.tongue: Relaxed; not involved in the nasal hum
mouthPosition.airflow: Nasal hum transitions into oral breathiness through the same gesture

sounds.englishAnchor: Say 'n' through your nose, then breathe 'h'
sounds.tip: Like 'mh' but with your tongue on the roof of your mouth (like 'n'). Nasal, then breathy.
sounds.practice: Step 1: Say 'n'. Step 2: Push air through your nose. Step 3: Open into the vowel. Combined: nh-asi.
sounds.commonMistake: Treating 'nh' like English 'n' + 'h' — keep one continuous breathy nasal into the vowel.

mouthPosition.lips: Neutral to slightly apart after the nasal release
mouthPosition.tongue: Blade at alveolar ridge for /n/, then breathy release into the vowel
mouthPosition.airflow: Nasal then oral with audible 'h' quality still riding the onset

sounds.englishAnchor: Start saying 'b' but let your lips vibrate into 'v'
sounds.tip: Your lips start closed (like 'b') then buzz open (like 'v'). It's a buzzy, vibrating 'b'.
sounds.practice: Step 1: Press lips together for 'b'. Step 2: Instead of popping open, let air buzz through into 'v'. Step 3: It should feel like a vibrating 'b'.
sounds.commonMistake: Stopping between /b/ and /v/ — it's one smooth labial buzz.

mouthPosition.lips: Start closed, then close-but-vibrating through the release into /v/
mouthPosition.airflow: Voiced buzz through the lips without a silent gap

sounds.englishAnchor: 'pf' in 'Pfizer' — or blowing out a candle with a 'p'
sounds.tip: You actually make this sound in English! Say 'Pfizer' or 'pfft!' (the dismissive sound).
sounds.practice: Step 1: Press lips together. Step 2: Release with a puff of air that becomes 'f'. Like a quiet spit.
sounds.commonMistake: Only saying /f/ without the lip pop — you need the stop + fricative release.

mouthPosition.lips: Closed bilabial stop, then part for voiceless labiodental fricative
mouthPosition.tongue: Low; lower lip meets upper teeth for /f/
mouthPosition.airflow: Sharp puff of air through the teeth after releasing the stop

sounds.englishAnchor: Start with 'ts' (like 'cats'), then add lip buzz 'v'
sounds.tip: This is just 'ts' + 'v' smashed together. Say 'cats' slowly: ca-ts. Now add a 'v' vibration: ts-v.
sounds.practice: Step 1: Say 'ts' (like end of 'cats'). Step 2: Let your bottom lip touch top teeth for 'v'. Step 3: Combine fast: tsv-uku.
sounds.commonMistake: Separating 'ts' and 'v' — keep one crisp cluster with lip rounding on the release.

mouthPosition.tongue: Raised for the alveolar affricate release, then groove for friction into /v/
mouthPosition.airflow: Voiceless stop + affricate friction, then voiced buzz at lips

sounds.tip: Nasal 'n' gliding into 'z'. You do this between words in English: 'in Zealand'.
sounds.practice: Say 'in' then 'z' without a pause: in-z → nz. Now: nz-eve.
sounds.commonMistake: Breaking between nasal and 'z' — glide straight from nasal airflow into the fricative.

mouthPosition.tongue: Tip at alveolar ridge for /n/, then groove for /z/
mouthPosition.airflow: Continuous from nasal to voiced fricative

sounds.tip: English has this sound in the middle of words (timber, lumber). Just move it to the front.
sounds.practice: Say 'timber'. Hear the 'mb'? Now drop 'ti': mb-ira.
sounds.commonMistake: Inserting a vowel before 'mb' — the nasal and stop are part of one onset.

mouthPosition.lips: Closed briefly for the oral stop after brief nasal flow
mouthPosition.tongue: Same as for /b/ — both lips, with nasal lead-in
mouthPosition.airflow: Very short nasal pre-stop, then voiced release

sounds.tip: Like 'nd' in 'under' but at the start. Very common — 'ndi-' means 'I'.
sounds.practice: Say 'under'. Hear the 'nd'? Drop the 'u': nd-iri.
sounds.commonMistake: Splitting 'n' and 'd' or adding 'uh' — treat as one syllable-onset cluster.

mouthPosition.tongue: Tip at alveolar ridge throughout nasal then stop
mouthPosition.airflow: Brief nasal flow into voiced stop release
